sources.quote: The Sabine Pass LNG Terminal in southwest Louisiana, which emitted 6.9 million tons of greenhouse gases and 8,780 tons of health-damaging “criteria” air pollutants in 2023, the most of any U.S. LNG terminal.
sources.searcher_note: Terminal Trouble report: Sabine Pass 6.9 Mt GHG in 2023 (lead says 6.26 Mt), largest US LNG terminal; no 2015 baseline or cross-facility rise ranking.

sources.quote: The seven LNG terminals operating in 2023 reported releasing 18.2 million tons of greenhouse gases that year, which was as much as 3.9 million cars and trucks driven for a year
sources.searcher_note: Seven-terminal 2023 total 18.2 Mt; lead's seven LNG facility IDs reach 16.48 Mt in 2023 (different facility set/accounting possible).

sources.quote: But the state’s first LNG terminal, Sabine Pass LNG, quickly became one of Louisiana’s largest sources of climate-warming pollution, releasing more greenhouse gases than the state’s biggest oil refineries.
sources.searcher_note: Verite News analysis of EPA/state records on Woodside Louisiana LNG; says Sabine Pass went from new to a top Louisiana GHG source; cites nearly 7 million tons per EPA.

sources.quote: The terminal’s emissions from the liquefaction process and other energy-intensive operations would be much higher than the nearly 7 million tons of greenhouse gases the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency says are emitted by the Sabine Pass terminal.
sources.searcher_note: Same article: EPA figure for Sabine Pass, current level only. Original Verite and Louisiana Illuminator URLs returned 403/blank to the fetcher.

sources.quote: In 2016, the U.S. exported its first tanker of liquified natural gas, or LNG, from Cheniere’s Energy’s Sabine Pass terminal in Cameron Parish.
sources.searcher_note: Earliest found: LNG terminals emitting more than estimated; Sabine Pass methane plumes stood out in optical-gas imaging. No GHGRP tonnage trend.

sources.quote: Over 33% reduction of scope 1 greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions intensity since startup of commercial LNG export operations in 2016.
sources.searcher_note: Company counter-framing: intensity per unit LNG fell even as absolute emissions grew; fits the lead's caveat that emissions track LNG shipped.

notes: Sources name Sabine Pass and put its current emissions near 7 Mt (EIP says 6.9 Mt in 2023 vs the lead's 6.26 Mt, about 10% apart), and say it quickly became a top Louisiana emitter. None found gives the 2015 baseline (0.18 Mt), the +6.08 Mt rise, or a rank-1-of-6,021 comparison across all GHGRP facilities. No Sabine Pass emissions-trend coverage dated after 2026-06-30 found (Grist 2026-08-27 and Chattanooga Times Free Press 2026-09-08 Plaquemines pieces only list Sabine Pass as an operating terminal). Inside Climate News (2025-04-16) covers LNG tanker shipping emissions quadrupling, a different measure.
